In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the OPEN Study, the FFQ led to substantial attenuation in estimated disease associations with protein and energy intakes, but that adjustment for energy attenuated the effect of the measurement error and that the 24HR is a poor reference instrument.
the OPEN data suggest that the errors in FFQs are highly correlated with true intake, but that the 24HRs have substantial measurement error that is independent of true intake.

the use of the FFQ as a dietary assessment method in nutritional epidemiologic studies leads to severe attenuation of the true relative risk of disease, and this attenuation is more pronounced for protein intake than for energy intake.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the OPEN study provides evidence that the FFQ is not an appropriate instrument for estimating absolute intakes of protein or energy.
FFQs can be useful tools to rank individuals by intake, but that their use to estimate the true relative risks of diet-disease association is problematic.

FFQs should not be used to estimate the absolute intake of energy or protein, and that the use of nutrient density or residual energy adjustment may be a more appropriate approach than energy adjustment alone for estimating the relative intake of protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of the FFQ as a dietary assessment tool in nutrition epidemiology is not a valid approach.
the use of 24HRs as the reference instrument to calibrate an FFQ can seriously underestimate the degree of attenuation that is expected from the measurement error.
the use of a 24-hour recall or multiple day dietary records as a reference instrument in the calibration of food frequency questionnaires can lead to severe underestimation of true attenuation.
